correctness.rationale: For k>=2, exactly k^2-t feasible edges give the three exact transition weights t(t-1), 2t(k-t), (k-t)^2. The first normalized factorial potential telescopes to an exact nonnegative correction. The second potential has conditional loss eta=2(k+2t-6)/[(k-2)(k^2-t)], bounded by 6/[k(k-1)]; this bounds E V_k between v and v(1-6/k). Comparing the exact correction weight (k+2)/(k^2-t) to 1/k and summing telescoping series yields the explicit error <=36v. All quantifiers include n>=2 and 0<=r<=n; the limit is uniform for 2<=r<=n and is not inferred from computation. originality.rationale: The claim is the evaluated uniform second-order logarithmic correction, with an explicit finite-size error bounded by a constant times r(r-1)/[n(n-1)(n+1)(n+2)] for every partial forbidden matching. Arnosti studies averaged random edge sets; Johnston et al. count perfect matchings; known full-crown greedy first-order bounds and recurrences do not imply the sharp uniform logarithmic coefficient or its simultaneous sparse/dense r dependence. The proof uses a second falling-factorial moment potential. Specific unresolved historical priority risks are recorded.
residual_risks: The two older general greedy-matching articles were not inspected in complete full text; their abstract scope suggests general bounds, but unindexed special-case overlap remains possible.
Published-record semantic search is not an exhaustive mathematical bibliography; additional historical sources may contain equivalent asymptotics.

The full-crown finite (k,t) recurrence and first-order bound are prior knowledge, not separately novel; the specific higher-order coefficient and uniform partial-deletion coverage are what are assessed.

value.rationale: The precise probability of a rare greedy matching failure in an almost-complete bipartite graph matters for contrasting sequential matching with counting derangements and for benchmarking randomized matching on dense constraints. The theorem classifies the effect of every partial forbidden matching at one sharp logarithmic order, uniformly from r=2 to r=n. The r=1 exact law pinpoints the onset of the second-order pair-interaction term. This simultaneously resolves sparse/dense deletion regimes and sharpens previously available full-crown O(log n/n^2) estimates, rather than substituting a parameter in a routine first-order formula.
